questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Massive retaliation and the New Look
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the New Look substituted nuclear firepower for conventional manpower.
questions.stem: Clear night over the ridge, my log records a long meditation on strategy: after 1953 Washington answered Soviet pressure with the doctrine of massive retaliation. Why did Eisenhower's New Look trade large conventional armies for a smaller nuclear force?

options.text: It promised to multiply American firepower at a fraction of the cost of matching Soviet manpower
Because thermonuclear weapons made every conventional weapon obsolete overnight
options.misconception: Believes nukes eliminated the need for conventional forces

options.text: Because Soviet leaders refused any negotiation until American troops were withdrawn from Europe
options.misconception: Assumes Soviet rigidity, not strategy, caused the change

options.text: Because Congress refused to finance troops but insisted on funding hundreds of bombers
options.misconception: Believes Congress forced the shift by cutting troop funding

questions.explanation: The New Look substituted cheaper nuclear firepower for expensive manpower to deter Soviet strength. Soviet obstinacy or congressional budget cuts do not explain a deliberate choice to gain an advantage at lower cost.
questions.hint: Which American advantage did the plan exploit?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify why the term quarantine was chosen over blockade in October 1962.
questions.stem: Cloudless November evening, I sketched the Atlantic and puzzled over a decision made in October 1962: the president ordered a naval 'quarantine' of Cuba. Why did the administration choose that word over 'blockade'?

options.text: Because a quarantine could be framed as an international police action rather than an act of war
Because the word blockade would have required a congressional declaration of war
options.misconception: Believes 'blockade' required a congressional war declaration

options.text: Because American lawyers insisted that only the word quarantine appeared in the treaty
options.misconception: Thinks the word choice came from a specific treaty clause

options.text: Because Soviet submarines would have refused to turn back under a blockade order
options.misconception: Believes Soviet submarines would ignore a blockade order

questions.explanation: Kennedy chose quarantine to present the halt as a police action against a dangerous shipment rather than an act of war. The alternatives misread a diplomatic signal as legal necessity or naval technicality.
questions.hint: Consider what the word was meant to avoid admitting.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Accuracy and the number of warheads
questions.learningObjective: Compare two arsenals by computing expected hits from quantity and accuracy.
questions.stem: Dust storm scoured the desert, hiding the horizon and my questions about warhead counts. I sketched two arsenals: Plan A had 1,000 warheads at 60 percent accuracy; Plan B had 400 warheads at 95 percent accuracy. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Plan A still lands more effective hits, so raw numbers can outweigh superior accuracy
Plan B lands more effective hits, so accuracy always outweighs sheer quantity
options.misconception: Believes precision alone guarantees more hits than many warheads

options.text: The plans are equivalent, since the product of the two figures is identical
options.misconception: Assumes both plans produce the same number of effective strikes

options.text: No comparison is possible, since accuracy percentages cannot be multiplied at all
options.misconception: Believes hit counts cannot be compared across different arsenals

questions.explanation: Plan A yields 600 expected hits against Plan B's 380, so sheer numbers could offset lower accuracy. The wrong readings treat precision as always decisive or the comparison as impossible.
questions.hint: Multiply warheads by accuracy before you decide.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a survivable second strike supports deterrence.
questions.stem: Fog rolled in from the valley tonight, and I thought about retaliation that survives an enemy's first blow. Explain how the argument for a second-strike capability shaped American defense planning after 1955.

answer.exemplar: A second-strike capability means that after absorbing an enemy first strike, the United States can still retaliate and inflict unacceptable damage. Because a first strike cannot eliminate that ability, an opponent gains little by striking first, so the capability supports deterrence. This reasoning drove investment in hardened silos, mobile missiles, submarine-launched systems, and eventually the triad that insulated the bomber, the ICBM, and the submarine.

questions.explanation: The question tests whether the student can explain how survivable retaliation changes the calculus of striking first. Answers that mention only larger bombs miss the point that the second strike must survive.
questions.hint: Focus on why striking first would be pointless.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Assess the significance of the underground testing exception in the 1963 treaty.

stimulus.body: Article I: No nuclear weapon tests shall be conducted in the atmosphere, in outer space, or under water. Testing underground is not prohibited by this treaty, and no party shall interfere with the activities of the other on its territory.

questions.stem: Frost silvered the dome, and I reread the clause below from the treaty signed in Moscow in 1963. What is the significance of the exception that underground testing was left outside the ban?

options.text: It allowed both powers to keep refining weapons designs while removing the visible fallout problem
It secretly required the United States to share every underground test with Soviet scientists
options.misconception: Believes the exception secretly obligated sharing of test data

options.text: It meant the Soviet Union had already abandoned testing at underground sites
options.misconception: Believes the exception proves the Soviets had stopped testing

options.text: It applied only to nuclear tests and deliberately excluded chemical and biological weapons
options.misconception: Believes the treaty quietly covered chemical and biological weapons

questions.explanation: Banning tests in air, space, and water removed visible fallout while underground work, which produced little, stayed legal. The treaty covered only nuclear tests, not chemical or biological ones.
questions.hint: Think about where fallout could not be contained.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize why the two-stage thermonuclear design changed deterrence after 1952.
questions.stem: Rain hammered the tin roof while I sketched the three-stage device that made a hundred-megaton warhead possible. Which combination best explains why the hydrogen bomb changed strategy after 1952?

options.text: A fusion stage boosted by a fission primary produced far more explosive yield than fission alone
The design used a smaller radioactive core, so each bomb stayed limited in blast radius
options.misconception: Believes the thermonuclear design reduced blast yield and size

options.text: It lowered production costs, letting the air force retire its bomber fleet
options.misconception: Believes the hydrogen bomb mainly served to cut military budgets

options.text: It was designed for submarine use, which is why its warhead was so compact
options.misconception: Believes thermonuclear warheads were built mainly for submarines

questions.explanation: A fission primary compressed a fusion fuel stage, multiplying yield far beyond any pure fission weapon. The distractors confuse the technical goal with budget or platform decisions.
questions.hint: Recall the two-stage arrangement of the design.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why Truman's 1948 order was carried forward by the Eisenhower administration.
questions.stem: Dawn came up clear over the observatory car park, and I thought about who sat behind federal desks. Why did the Eisenhower administration continue to carry out Truman's order requiring equal opportunity in federal employment?

options.text: Because the order remained the legal basis for equal opportunity in federal employment
Because the order had already been repealed by Congress in 1954
options.misconception: Believes Congress repealed the order in the mid-1950s

options.text: Because the Supreme Court had already ruled all employment segregation unconstitutional
options.misconception: Believes the Court had already banned all segregation in hiring

options.text: Because federal employees had no legal protection against discriminatory employers
options.misconception: Believes federal workers lacked any legal protection at work

questions.explanation: Truman's 1948 order remained the legal commitment to equal opportunity in federal employment, and Eisenhower enforced rather than abandoned it. The distractors invent a repeal or a ruling that never came.
questions.hint: Which legal commitment was still in force?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how the federal loyalty program operated in practice.
questions.stem: Wind rattled the dome shutter, which reminded me of how easily a government can make a list of names. How did the federal loyalty program of the late 1940s operate in practice?

options.text: Federal agencies held hearings to determine whether employees had ties to the Communist Party
Congress passed a law making party membership itself a criminal offence for all citizens
options.misconception: Believes membership itself became a crime for all citizens

options.text: A single secret ballot in each election allowed voters to remove suspected communists
options.misconception: Believes voters secretly voted to remove suspected communists

options.text: Communist Party leaders were required to register their members with the justice department
options.misconception: Believes party members had to register themselves with prosecutors

questions.explanation: Loyalty boards held administrative hearings on employees' affiliations and could dismiss them as security risks. The distractors confuse employment screening with criminal law or with party registration.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Massive retaliation and the New Look
questions.learningObjective: Interpret defence figures showing quality replacing quantity under the New Look.
questions.stem: Heat shimmer over the parking lot at noon, and I tallied figures from an old defence briefing: the New Look held the defence share of the budget near 13 percent while cutting Army divisions from about 20 to 16. What does this combination show?

options.text: The administration traded manpower and divisions for a qualitatively different force built on nuclear firepower
The administration expanded the conventional army while shifting money to missile research
options.misconception: Believes conventional divisions grew during the New Look years

options.text: The administration cut defence spending sharply and returned the money to domestic programmes
options.misconception: Believes total defence spending fell sharply under Eisenhower

options.text: The administration kept conventional divisions constant and merely renamed the older forces
options.misconception: Believes divisions were unchanged and only their names changed

questions.explanation: Fewer divisions with a stable defence share means quality replaced quantity: fewer conventional troops backed by much greater nuclear capability. The distractors contradict the arithmetic of the figures.
questions.hint: Read what fewer divisions with steady spending implies.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the quarantine shaped Soviet decision-making in October 1962.
questions.stem: Icy morning, my breath fogged the logbook while I considered the blockade. Explain how the Kennedy administration's decision to quarantine Cuba in October 1962 affected the Soviet calculation.

answer.exemplar: The quarantine forced Moscow to choose between withdrawing the missiles and risking a naval confrontation the Kremlin could not control. Kennedy paired the naval cordon with a public warning that the United States would respond to any Soviet missile launch from Cuba, which forced the leaders to remove the weapons while saving face. The decision worked because it raised the cost of confrontation without removing the option of a quiet retreat.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student links the quarantine to Soviet decision-making under nuclear shadow. Answers that treat it as costless or as luck miss the coercion logic.
questions.hint: Ask what choice the cordon forced on the Soviet leaders.

questions.topic: Accuracy and the number of warheads
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fewer, more accurate weapons could be more dangerous than a larger force.
questions.stem: Moonless night, only the planets visible, and I mapped the arithmetic of deterrence. Why did strategists in the 1960s conclude that fewer but more accurate weapons could be more dangerous than a larger, less accurate force?

options.text: Because accuracy let a few warheads destroy the specific targets an opponent valued most
Because inaccurate bombs wasted money and the air force simply wanted cheaper weapons
options.misconception: Believes the shift was purely about cost saving

options.text: Because accurate warheads could be delivered without any need for bombers or missiles
options.misconception: Believes accuracy removed the need for delivery systems

options.text: Because opponents believed accurate weapons were being built for use in Europe only
options.misconception: Believes accuracy implied a fixed European-only targeting doctrine

questions.explanation: Greater accuracy let a small arsenal destroy valued targets, so the deterrent survived a surprise strike. The wrong answers reduce the shift to budgets, delivery systems, or geography.
questions.hint: Think about what few but accurate warheads could still destroy.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret hearing and removal figures to characterise loyalty board procedure.
questions.stem: Mud season again, so I stayed indoors and read about the loyalty system. Suppose a loyalty board reviewed 400 federal employees, questioned 90, and removed 25. What does the gap between questioning and removal suggest about the procedure?

options.text: Most questioned employees were cleared, so the boards relied on hearings rather than automatic removal
Every questioned employee was dismissed, so the numbers reveal the board's target quota
options.misconception: Believes questioning always ended in dismissal for every case

options.text: Only a quarter of the workforce was examined, so the review was narrow and unthorough
options.misconception: Believes questioning a small share proves the review was weak

options.text: The removals were so few that the program had no real effect on the workforce
options.misconception: Believes few removals prove the loyalty program changed nothing

questions.explanation: Only a quarter of those questioned were dismissed, so boards judged individual cases rather than dismissing on suspicion. The distractors invent a quota or read low removals as ineffectiveness.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the escalation risk that most worried military advisers in 1962.
questions.stem: Silence on the hill tonight, only the chronometer ticking, and I weighed the risk of the naval quarantine. Which factor most worried American military advisers in October 1962?

options.text: A naval clash could escalate uncontrollably into a nuclear war between the superpowers
Soviet subs could not be detected in Cuban waters and might fire on quarantine ships
options.misconception: Believes submarine detection was the central worry

options.text: The quarantine fleet would run out of fuel before the crisis ended
options.misconception: Believes the real risk was running out of fuel for the fleet

options.text: Congress had not authorized the use of force for a blockade of any kind
options.misconception: Believes advisers feared a lack of congressional authorization

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare three delivery systems by computing surviving weapon strength.
questions.stem: Smoke from the neighbour's chimney drifted past my window as I considered survivability figures: a bomber force of 500 aircraft with 50 percent surviving, a silo force of 400 missiles with 90 percent surviving, and a submarine force of 90 boats with 80 percent surviving. Which system survives best?

options.text: The silo force, because 360 of its 400 missiles survive a first strike
The bomber force, because 500 aircraft is the largest number in the comparison
options.misconception: Believes the biggest inventory always survives a first strike

options.text: The submarine force, because 72 surviving boats are easier to hide
options.misconception: Believes fewer survivors is better because they hide better

options.text: The systems tie, because survivability percentages alone decide the outcome
options.misconception: Believes survivability percentages alone settle the comparison

questions.explanation: Multiplying inventory by survivability gives 250, 360 and 72 surviving weapons, so the silo force retaliates hardest. Counting inventory alone rewards the force most likely to be destroyed.
questions.hint: Multiply each inventory by its survivability rate.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1963 treaty was a limited measure rather than disarmament.
questions.stem: Thunder shook the tin roof and I started writing about the treaty that stopped testing in the air. Explain why the 1963 limited test ban was described as a step short of a full disarmament agreement.

answer.exemplar: The 1963 treaty banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space, and under water, but it left underground testing legal and created no limit on the number of warheads. Both superpowers kept designing new weapons and testing them underground. It was therefore a practical measure that removed the fallout and propaganda value of visible testing while leaving the arms race itself substantially intact.

questions.explanation: The item checks whether the student distinguishes a partial measure from full disarmament. Answers claiming the treaty ended testing or capped weapons miss the underground exemption.
questions.hint: Notice what the treaty deliberately left permitted.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early thermonuclear devices were larger than the weapons they replaced.
questions.stem: Twilight at 9 p.m. and I was still puzzling over a technical worry: why were the first hydrogen bombs so much larger than the plutonium bombs they replaced?

options.text: The staged design demanded heavy, complex machinery, so early models were unwieldy
Fission fuel is always lighter than fusion fuel, so weight was the only constraint
options.misconception: Believes fusion fuel weighed more than fission material

options.text: Because engineers believed smaller hydrogen bombs would never be stable enough to work
options.misconception: Believes engineers doubted small hydrogen bombs would work

options.text: Because the air force insisted on one bomb per bomber for the whole program
options.misconception: Believes air force policy alone set the early weapon size

questions.explanation: Staging a fusion secondary around a fission primary required heavy cooling and complex assembly, so early devices were large. Later engineering, including cryogenic fuels, made them small enough for missiles.
questions.hint: Consider the engineering demands of a two-stage device.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Accuracy and the number of warheads
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a falling warhead count alongside a rising accuracy rate.

stimulus.body: Entry: The briefing officer drew two curves on the board. The left curve showed warhead numbers falling from 20,000 in 1955 to 8,000 in 1960 while the right curve showed accuracy climbing sharply. He underlined a sentence: the size of the deterrent depends on what can be delivered, not on what exists.

questions.stem: Warm afternoon, the dome too hot to open, so I worked out what the briefing officer meant. Which trend best explains the shift described in the log entry?

options.text: As missiles and submarines delivered weapons accurately, fewer warheads could hold the same deterrent
As warhead numbers fell, the accuracy of each weapon rose because of warmer summers
options.misconception: Believes the accuracy curve reflected a seasonal factor

options.text: The falling numbers show that the United States was losing the arms race to the Soviets
options.misconception: Believes fewer warheads signalled a losing race

options.text: The rising accuracy curve means bombs had become physically lighter to carry
options.misconception: Believes accuracy meant bombs weighed less

questions.explanation: When delivery became accurate enough to hit hard targets, a smaller arsenal still threatened the damage an opponent cared about. The wrong options invent a seasonal cause, a lost race, or lighter bombs.
questions.hint: Ask what matters more to a deterrent: count or effect.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesize how the strategic triad provided a survivable second strike.
questions.stem: Bitter wind across the observing floor and I began a note on how a deterrent survives. Which combination best explains how the United States built a credible second-strike capability in the late 1950s and early 1960s?

A single enormous bomber fleet, so that any surviving aircraft could carry the whole arsenal
options.misconception: Believes one platform type could carry the whole deterrent

options.text: Dense armies in Europe and Korea, which absorbed the first blow before nuclear response
options.misconception: Believes conventional armies supplied the nuclear second strike

options.misconception: Believes overseas stockpiles alone deterred an attack

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the loyalty program targeted federal employment rather than outlawing parties.

Because the Constitution prevented the government from regulating private political groups

More conventional divisions, a smaller nuclear stockpile, and reliance on negotiated arms limits
options.misconception: Believes the New Look meant more troops and fewer bombs

options.text: Fewer conventional divisions, a smaller nuclear stockpile, and reliance on European alliance politics
options.misconception: Believes the New Look cut nuclear weapons and relied on alliances

options.misconception: Believes the New Look expanded the army and cut US commitments

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the missile withdrawal bargain as a face-saving outcome.
questions.stem: Sunrise lit the antenna field and I finally understood the arithmetic of brinkmanship. The Soviet Union cancelled two of its planned missiles while the United States pledged not to invade Cuba, and inspection teams entered the island within a week. What does that exchange show?

A total American victory, since the Soviets simply surrendered under the threat of war
options.misconception: Believes the outcome was an unallied Soviet capitulation

options.misconception: Believes the pledge not to invade shows Soviet supremacy

options.misconception: Believes the outcome proves the blockade had no effect

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute the ratio of thermonuclear yield to fission yield.
questions.stem: Dry season dust on the lens, so I cleaned it and thought about yields. In 1952 the first successful thermonuclear test yielded about 10 megatons, while a comparable fission weapon of the 1940s yielded about 0.02 megatons. Roughly how many times larger was the thermonuclear yield?

options.text: About 500 times larger, showing how completely fusion changed the scale of destruction
About 50 times larger, showing a modest but real improvement over fission
options.misconception: Believes the improvement over fission was only fiftyfold

options.text: About 5,000 times larger, showing an effect larger than any conceivable weapon
options.misconception: Believes the yield was five thousand times greater

options.text: About 5 times larger, showing that thermonuclear yield stayed close to fission levels
options.misconception: Believes thermonuclear yields were barely above fission yields

questions.explanation: Ten megatons divided by 0.02 is about 500, a leap of scale rather than a marginal gain. The distractors misplace the decimal and so understate or overstate how completely fusion changed destructive range.
questions.hint: Divide the larger yield by the smaller one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what Truman's 1948 executive order required of federal employment.
questions.stem: The cat knocked the chart off the bench, and I sat down to consider the order that reshaped federal hiring. What did Truman's 1948 executive order require?

The immediate admission of Black workers into every state and local government in the nation
options.misconception: Believes the order applied to state and local governments directly

options.misconception: Believes a single system is cheaper and so better

options.text: Only submarine-launched weapons could survive a first strike, so others were phased out

options.text: The cost of defense mattered more than the ability to retaliate after being struck
options.misconception: Believes the memo treated cost as the decisive factor

questions.explanation: The memo argues that spreading delivery across systems removes the single point of failure an enemy must defeat. The distractors contradict it by favouring one system or making cost the strategic criterion.
questions.hint: Ask what an enemy must defeat to stop retaliation.

questions.stem: Storm watch tonight meant no observing, so I read about the security program and thought about how employees were judged. Explain how hearings and compelled disclosure functioned in the federal loyalty program.

answer.exemplar: Employees were asked to disclose their affiliations and to answer questions about them, and where the answers looked inadequate they were brought before a loyalty board. The board weighed the evidence and could either clear the employee or declare the person a security risk and remove them from federal service. The process mixed a hearing with a demand for information, so the employee's own testimony, not only outside accusations, became part of the case against them.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student can explain how disclosure and hearings decided individual cases. Answers about secret files alone, or formal trials alone, miss the board mechanism.
questions.hint: Consider what the employee supplied and who judged it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how mobile systems protected the American retaliatory force.
questions.stem: In the library archive I found a pamphlet about mobile missiles and asked why mobility mattered. Explain how mobile systems changed the American approach to a survivable retaliatory force.

answer.exemplar: Mobile missiles cannot be found and destroyed in a fixed launch position. questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student explains why mobility protects a retaliatory force rather than describing mobile missiles. Answers that call mobility decisive without the search problem miss the point.
questions.hint: Consider what an enemy must find before it can fire.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student connects detection and warning time to the survivability of a retaliatory force. Answers that treat continental defence as a separate problem miss the strategic link.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the budgetary argument for greater missile accuracy.
questions.stem: A retired Air Force officer at the club spoke about accuracy as a money problem. Why did the air force argue that more accurate missiles were cheaper overall?

options.text: A missile that reliably hit a hardened target removed the need to fire several warheads at it
Accurate missiles used less fuel, so aircraft flew farther without refuelling
options.misconception: Believes accuracy mainly saved fuel

options.text: Accuracy allowed the air force to keep its bomber fleet in permanent peacetime rotation
options.misconception: Believes accuracy kept the bomber fleet on peacetime rotation

options.text: Precision missiles required no launchers, because they could be fired from aircraft only
options.misconception: Believes precision missiles needed no launchers at all

questions.explanation: If one reliably aimed warhead could destroy a hardened target, the military no longer had to shoot several at it, lowering the cost of a given level of destruction. The distractors misplace the saving in fuel or launcher design.
questions.hint: Consider how many warheads a single hardened target required.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the mutual interest that led both superpowers to sign the 1963 ban.
questions.stem: The town historical society showed a newspaper clipping about the treaty signed in Moscow in 1963. Why did both superpowers sign a ban on testing in the atmosphere, outer space, and under water?

options.text: Each side could no longer gain from visible testing, and each feared the political cost of fallout
Because the treaty also ended all underground testing for both nations
options.misconception: Believes the treaty also barred underground testing

options.text: Because the Soviet Union wanted to protect its own atmosphere from American surveillance
options.misconception: Believes the treaty was about protecting Soviet airspace

options.text: Because the United States had already built underground facilities the treaty protected
options.misconception: Believes the treaty shielded American underground facilities

questions.explanation: The superpowers had mastered the weapons that mattered, so visible testing bought little advantage while fallout created political costs at home and abroad. The alternatives misread the treaty's scope or its purpose.
questions.hint: Weigh what each side gained and lost from visible tests.

questions.learningObjective: Compute usable warheads after applying a launcher loss rate.
questions.stem: While fixing the drive motor, I found a metal tag stamped with a range figure and wondered about magazine loading. If each missile carried two warheads and 40 percent of a 500-launcher silo force could not be used after an attack, how many warheads remained in usable condition?

options.text: 600 warheads, because only 60 percent of launchers remained usable and each carried two
400 warheads, because 40 percent of the 1,000 warheads were lost with the unusable launchers
options.misconception: Believes the loss rate applied to warheads rather than launchers

options.text: 200 warheads, because only the launchers with two warheads survived a first strike
options.misconception: Believes only fully loaded launchers counted as surviving

options.text: 1,000 warheads, because every launcher kept both warheads regardless of the damage
options.misconception: Believes damaged launchers still launched their warheads

questions.explanation: Sixty percent of 500 launchers is 300 usable launchers, and two warheads each gives 600 usable warheads. The distractors apply the loss rate to warheads or ignore the damage entirely.
questions.hint: Apply the loss rate to launchers first.

Its power came from a simple core, so the size of the device was mostly administrative
options.misconception: Believes the device was simple and its size administrative

options.text: Its power came from an ordinary fission bomb that was simply dropped harder
options.misconception: Believes hydrogen bombs were fission bombs dropped harder

questions.learningObjective: Synthesize how the federal loyalty system operated during the 1950s.
questions.stem: My astronomy club's centennial lecture asked how a free society treated its own citizens during the cold war. Which combination best describes the federal loyalty program as it operated in the 1950s?

options.text: Executive orders created security standards, hearings judged individual employees, and fears of subversion spread
Congress passed a criminal statute making party membership a federal offence for every citizen
options.misconception: Believes membership itself was made a federal crime

options.text: Federal examiners supervised elections in counties where suspected communists lived
options.misconception: Believes federal voting examiners screened employees

options.text: State governors were given power to dismiss any federal employee living in their states
options.misconception: Believes governors were empowered to dismiss federal employees

questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1948 order set policy while leaving implementation to departments.

stimulus.body: Reporter: Does the order force the military to admit Negro enlisted men into every unit and every officers' club? Press secretary: It declares a national policy of equal opportunity, and the departments are directed to carry it out. Details of implementation are theirs to work out.

questions.stem: A visiting professor's talk on orbital mechanics reminded me of an old press conference. What does the exchange indicate about how the 1948 order operated?

options.text: It set a national standard of equal opportunity and left the mechanics of implementation to the departments
It prescribed detailed rules for every mess hall and officers' club in the country
options.misconception: Believes the order prescribed rules for every facility

options.text: It applied only to civilian hiring and excluded the armed forces entirely
options.misconception: Believes the order excluded the armed forces

options.text: It required each state legislature to rewrite its own civil service rules
options.misconception: Believes state legislatures had to rewrite civil service rules

questions.explanation: The exchange shows a broad national standard combined with administrative discretion, as departments worked out the details. The distractors misstate the order's detail, its scope or the level of government responsible.
questions.hint: Notice who was left to work out the details.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Accuracy and the number of warheads
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the contrast between volume and precision in a documentary excerpt.

stimulus.body: Entry: Our old chart compared two doctrines. One spread a large stock of bombs over many targets, hoping some would land. The other aimed fewer weapons at the few places where an opponent's strength actually lived, and trusted that accuracy to do the rest.

questions.stem: Over the radio, a documentary described two ways of thinking about deterrence. Which interpretation of the contrast is best supported?

options.text: Precision concentrates force on an opponent's decisive assets, while volume accepts many misses
Precision spreads damage evenly across a country, while volume focuses on one city
options.misconception: Believes precision spreads damage while volume concentrates it

options.text: Precision reduces the effect of each weapon, so more shots are needed to achieve the same result
options.misconception: Believes precision reduces each weapon's effect

options.text: Precision matters only for small weapons, so large bombs could still be fired blindly
options.misconception: Believes precision mattered only for small weapons

questions.explanation: The contrast maps onto targeting logic: many bombs accept losses to reach broad targets, while accurate weapons concentrate force on the assets that make an opponent dangerous. The distractors reverse the effects or restrict precision's value.
questions.hint: Ask where each doctrine concentrates its force.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Massive retaliation and the New Look
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the sequence from massive retaliation to the New Look to flexible response.
questions.stem: Finally the sky cleared and I could sit with my last question about doctrine and doctrine after doctrine. Which combination best captures the sequence of American strategy from massive retaliation to the New Look to flexible response?

options.text: A threat of overwhelming force, then reliance on strategic superiority, then options short of nuclear war
A policy of no retaliation at all, then overwhelming force, then a return to exclusive conventional defence
options.misconception: Believes the sequence began with a policy of no retaliation

options.text: Overwhelming force, then a retreat from nuclear planning to conventional force as the only answer
options.misconception: Believes the New Look abandoned nuclear planning entirely

options.text: Options short of nuclear war, then overwhelming force, then exclusive reliance on alliance commitments
options.misconception: Believes the sequence began with flexible response

questions.explanation: Massive retaliation promised overwhelming force, the New Look built it while cutting conventional divisions, and later strategy added options below full nuclear use. The distractors reverse the order or claim nuclear planning was abandoned.
questions.hint: Order the three stages by when they mattered.
